prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength allow clock comparisons at the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep a single prize part for the optical lattice clock, credited to Katori and Ye. After the first round the scientific case looks to me unchanged, and the exchange has made the credit sharper. The new idea is a physical mechanism, not a better apparatus: at the magic wavelength the lattice shifts the two clock levels equally, so thousands of atoms can be held tightly (the Lamb-Dicke regime) and interrogated together without Stark shift or recoil. Neither of the earlier prizes did that. The comb (2005) made optical frequencies countable, and single-ion control (2012) gave a clean but single absorber with weak signal. Many-atom interrogation with a cancelled light shift is what brought stability and accuracy to the 1e-18 level, where millimetre-scale gravitational redshift is resolved, drifts of constants are bounded and dark-matter couplings can be searched for. The result is reproduced and compared across independent laboratories, and the committee can describe it as a statement about how time behaves in nature as well as a better clock. I would write the citation around the lattice and the magic wavelength, not around timekeeping in general, which answers the chair's first question and the worry about incrementalism. I do not think any member has made a case that makes a second part necessary, and I could not support one that needs a fourth name.
statement.case_against: The overlap objection has not gone away, and I should say plainly that it is a judgment about taste, not a fact I can settle. Ye shared the 2005 prize, so the committee would honour the same laboratory family twice, and the 2005 and 2012 prizes sit close in the same line of precision spectroscopy. A reader can fairly say that the lattice clock is a decisive step but still a step. The attribution is also not airtight: Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Derevianko, Oates and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups made real contributions, and the 1e-18 record was reached with several groups pushing each other. Olsson's point also stands: if Ye's contribution is mainly performance on an idea that Katori proposed and first demonstrated, the committee must be able to say why the second is a distinct prize-worthy step and not a second group doing it much better. Finally, my own closeness to atomic structure theory could make me read the conceptual depth of the result too generously, and Pearce is right that broad support partly reflects clean attribution, which is not the same as scientific weight.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Katori and Ye are credited for the same achievement, and whether the prize rewards the original work or a second group that did it much better.
responses.response: This is the most useful challenge in the round and it changes how I would word the citation, not the credit. As I recall the sequence, Katori and collaborators proposed the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock in the early-to-mid 2000s, and Ye's group then showed what the scheme could do: the many-body clock, record stability and the 1e-18 systematic uncertainty. I have not checked dates against the record, so I would ask the committee's secretariat to confirm them before the vote. I would not call Ye's work merely a second group doing it better, because reaching 1e-18 required new understanding of density shifts, blackbody radiation and lattice-induced effects, and that is what turned a promising scheme into a platform for tests of nature. I think the right reading is one achievement, invention and realization, with two decisive steps. If a member's support depends on separating them, the citation should keep both words, and I would not shift credit toward the realizer alone.

responses.point: Pearce observes that broad support may reflect clean attribution rather than scientific weight, treats the Higgs (B001) as arguably heavier, and keeps B001 or B059 as fallback if Ye's 2005 prize is felt to be disqualifying.
responses.response: I take the point about attribution versus weight seriously, and I defer to him and Johansson on how heavy the Higgs discovery is. I do not think weight and clean attribution are independent, though: a prize that cannot name its laureates without an arbitrary choice among four people from two collaborations is a weaker public statement, however large the discovery, and the 2013 prize already honoured the mechanism. On Ye and 2005, I would ask what the prize is for. Ye shared the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and precision spectroscopy; the 2026 citation would be for a different invention, the neutral-atom lattice with the magic wavelength. I do not see the Nobel statutes or our practice making a returning laureate disqualifying, as long as the new work is distinct. If the committee did decide that, I would rather see Katori alone than switch the field, but I would not recommend it because it loses the realization.

responses.point: Mehlig lists the earlier recognitions (1989, 1997, 2001, 2005, 2012) and notes that KPZ (B042) has deeper conceptual reach but almost no support and a messy attribution; he also asks whether the citation should be phrased around invention and realization.
responses.response: I agree with his wording suggestion and have adopted it. On his list, I would separate the earlier prizes by what they recognised: laser cooling and trapping, the comb, and ion control are tools and principles that the lattice clock uses, whereas the magic-wavelength lattice is a new principle for combining many atoms with an undisturbed transition. That is a reason to count it as additional, not repeated. I respect his view that KPZ reaches deeper, and as a theorist I find the exactly solved universality attractive. But I judge a prize case by whether the credit can be stated cleanly and the result checked by other laboratories, and the Parisi problem he describes makes a three-name KPZ prize hard to defend this year.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether the pending redefinition of the second should make the committee wait, and whether the citation should mention the other strontium and ytterbium groups.
responses.response: I do not think the redefinition argues for waiting. The scientific achievement is the clock performance, comparisons across laboratories and the tests of redshift and constants, all of which exist now; the redefinition is a metrological decision that follows the science and may take years more, and a Nobel prize should not depend on a standards body's timetable. Waiting also risks nothing being clearer, only more groups being added to the discussion. On the other groups, I would not name them in the citation, because the three-person limit already makes naming impossible and a citation that lists people stops reading like a statement of the discovery. I would instead let the phrase 'invention and realization of optical lattice clocks' do the work, and accept that the recognition of SYRTE, PTB and NIST is through the field, not the diploma. I also hold my view that B037 (squeezed light) is a respectable alternative but not a companion part.

responses.point: Johansson moves his own circuit QED (B054) to an alternative, asks whether superconducting circuits are already covered by the 2025 prize, and says he should be recused from B054.
responses.response: I appreciate the clear recusal statement, and I would ask the chair to record it and treat his comments on B054 as information, not advocacy. On the substance, I agree that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes a further superconducting-circuit prize this year harder to argue as a separate achievement, which is one reason I do not want to see a second part built on B054. It is a clean illustration of the principle I apply to B013: it needs a result that adds a different physical idea, not a better device in a family that has just been recognised.

uncertainties: I still rely on my own recollection of the early strontium lattice-clock dates (Katori's proposal and first demonstration in the early-to-mid 2000s, Ye's later accuracy records); I have not verified them against the literature and would want the secretariat to check them before a final vote.

Whether colleagues outside atomic physics will accept that the magic-wavelength lattice is a new principle and not an extension of the comb and ion-control prizes; I think it is, but this is a judgment on which reasonable members differ.
Whether a returning laureate (Ye, 2005) is a procedural or practical problem for the committee and the Academy; I do not think so, but I do not know past practice well.

Whether a second part is wanted by anyone as a condition of their vote; if so, I see no candidate (B050, B037, B001) with an attribution inside the three-person limit that I can defend, and B050 still requires a choice among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger and Zoller.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and work in atomic many-body theory, so I am professionally close to the atomic-physics subfield of B013 and B050. I have no personal or institutional connection with Katori or Ye that I know of, and no conflict requiring recusal on B013. My disclosure is unchanged since round 1. I note the chair's summary records that Johansson and Olsson plan to treat B054 and B015 as recusal topics, and I support that.
